repoFacts: Fifteen public tools share src/mcp-server.js -> src/index.js:createGeminiSession() -> src/browser.js:ensureBrowser() -> src/gemini-ops.js, so route risk is dominated by how much of that chain can be preserved.

gemini_browser_info intentionally bypasses createGeminiSession() and talks to daemon HTTP endpoints directly, so daemon semantics are part of the public capability baseline rather than an internal detail.
The browser stack depends on puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth in both src/browser.js and src/daemon/engine.js, plus Chrome profile cloning in src/daemon/engine.js before first launch.

The current lifecycle is a detached daemon spawned with stdio ignored, a /health probe, GET /browser/acquire, GET /browser/status, POST /browser/release, and TTL-based browser reuse plus disconnect() without browser close.
Task 2 froze machine mode to exactly one JSON envelope on stdout; current contamination hazards come from browser/daemon console logging and the process.stdout polling pattern in src/demo2.js.

weights.name: Delivery risk
weights.reason: This migration blocks later implementation work, so the route must minimize parity and contract regression risk first.

weights.name: Reuse of existing Puppeteer/CDP logic
weights.reason: The current product behavior already lives in Node automation code, stealth wiring, and daemon lifecycle helpers.

weights.name: Packaging quality
weights.reason: A native CLI should package cleanly for end users, but packaging alone does not outweigh parity or machine-mode safety.

weights.name: Runtime performance
weights.reason: CPU and startup efficiency matter, but browser automation latency still dominates many commands.

weights.name: Maintainability
weights.reason: The chosen route becomes the long-term codebase and must stay operable after the migration freeze.

weights.name: Testability
weights.reason: Later tasks need route-neutral contract, parity, integration, and smoke coverage that can run in CI.

weights.name: Release complexity
weights.reason: Publishing should stay reproducible across macOS, Linux, and Windows without brittle multi-step handoffs.

weights.name: Daemon and lifecycle migration complexity
weights.reason: The current detached daemon, HTTP API surface, and browser-info exception are major architecture constraints.

daemonStrategyOptions.summary: Keep the detached daemon topology and treat it as a private subsystem of the native CLI.
daemonStrategyOptions.repoFit: Best parity fit because browser-info already relies on /health and /browser/acquire semantics, and TTL reuse matches the current disconnect() behavior.

daemonStrategyOptions.summary: Fold browser lifecycle into each CLI invocation and remove the detached daemon boundary.
daemonStrategyOptions.repoFit: Looks simple on paper, but it drops TTL reuse, makes browser-info semantics awkward, and reintroduces cold starts on every command.

daemonStrategyOptions.summary: Replace the current daemon with a new lifecycle supervisor implemented by the chosen route.
daemonStrategyOptions.repoFit: Preserves the idea of long-lived browser ownership, but requires re-creating acquire/status/release behavior, signal handling, stealth wiring, and profile bootstrap logic.

routes.label: Go rewrite
routes.summary: Rewrite the CLI and browser runtime in Go, and replace the current Node daemon with a Go-native browser supervisor.
repoFacts: Go would need to re-create the current Puppeteer-plus-stealth behavior even though the exact implementation today lives in Node libraries.
The route would also need to replace the detached daemon HTTP contract that browser-info currently uses directly.
Chrome profile clone bootstrap from src/daemon/engine.js would need a new implementation and new failure handling.

daemonStrategy.summary: Replace the detached Node daemon with a Go-native supervisor that exposes internal acquire/status/release behavior to the CLI.
reasons: Keeping the Node daemon would undercut the point of a full Go rewrite.
Folding the lifecycle would lose TTL reuse and make browser-info parity harder.
A replacement supervisor can preserve the long-lived browser model, but only after reimplementing current lifecycle semantics.

strengths: Best single-binary packaging story once the rewrite is complete.
Good runtime efficiency and strong distribution tooling.
risks: Low reuse of existing Puppeteer, stealth, and Chrome-profile logic.
High architecture risk because machine-mode stdout guarantees and daemon behavior must be rebuilt while parity work is still pending.
Requires a fresh implementation for the current browser-info direct-daemon capability.

routes.label: Rust rewrite
routes.summary: Rewrite the CLI in Rust and fold browser lifecycle into each command instead of carrying forward the detached daemon as a first-class runtime service.
repoFacts: Rust can produce strong native artifacts, but the current browser automation behavior is not implemented in Rust today and would need net-new CDP and stealth choices.
Folding the lifecycle conflicts with the current browser-info behavior, which expects daemon health and acquire semantics rather than a one-shot process-only model.
Task 2 machine mode still needs airtight stdout discipline, so a rewrite does not remove the need for explicit stderr-only diagnostics handling.

daemonStrategy.summary: Fold lifecycle ownership into each command process and drop the detached daemon boundary in exchange for a single-process runtime model.
reasons: This route chases the cleanest native packaging story and avoids shipping a second long-lived process on purpose.
The cost is losing current TTL-based reuse and forcing browser startup or reconnect decisions into every command.
browser-info would need a new compatibility story because there is no standing daemon endpoint to inspect anymore.

strengths: Strong native packaging and excellent long-term systems-level performance ceilings.
Potentially good maintainability after the rewrite if a full Rust browser architecture already existed.
risks: Lowest near-term reuse because the current automation stack is entirely Node-based.
Folding lifecycle removes a proven operational boundary while parity and contract migration are still incomplete.
Highest daemon/lifecycle mismatch because current direct-daemon diagnostics would need replacement semantics.

routes.label: Native CLI plus existing Node core
routes.summary: Build a native CLI shell while keeping the current Node browser and daemon core as the first migration target behind a private interface.
repoFacts: This route preserves the current shared runtime chain used by fifteen tools and keeps browser-info on the same direct daemon semantics it already exposes.
The existing Node core already contains the stealth plugin, Chrome profile clone bootstrap, TTL lifecycle, and CDP session logic that define today's behavior.
The main remaining contract work is packaging and process boundary control so all daemon or browser logs stay off stdout in machine mode.

daemonStrategy.summary: Keep the detached daemon model, but make it a private internal subsystem of the native CLI with stderr-only diagnostics and no public MCP dependency.
reasons: The current detached acquire/disconnect/TTL lifecycle already matches how most commands keep the browser alive between invocations.
browser-info already depends on daemon HTTP endpoints directly, so preserving the daemon avoids inventing compatibility shims before parity work begins.
Keeping the daemon lets the native wrapper focus on machine-mode envelopes, exit codes, and packaging first while reusing proven browser behavior.

strengths: Highest reuse of current automation logic, daemon semantics, stealth integration, and Chrome-profile bootstrap behavior.
Lowest delivery risk because the migration can wrap existing behavior before replacing internals.
Keeps the browser-info exception intact instead of forcing an immediate redesign.
risks: Packaging quality is weaker than a pure Go or Rust rewrite because the native CLI still carries a Node core in the near term.
Later tasks must aggressively redirect daemon/browser logging to stderr to protect the single JSON stdout envelope.
Release automation still has to supervise a mixed runtime instead of a pure single-language artifact.

finalDecision.selectionSummary: Choose the native CLI plus existing Node core route first, because it preserves the current browser/daemon behavior while the new CLI wrapper absorbs the machine-mode and packaging transition.
reasons: It is the only route that keeps both the dominant createGeminiSession runtime chain and the browser-info direct-daemon exception without immediate rearchitecture.
It reuses the current stealth plugin setup, Chrome profile clone bootstrap, TTL lifecycle, and detached daemon flow instead of re-deriving them under time pressure.
It localizes the first migration wave to native wrapper concerns: one JSON stdout envelope, stderr-only diagnostics, exit codes, packaging, and test harness integration.
The packaging downside is real, but the weighted matrix still leaves this route far ahead because parity and delivery risk are the blocking constraints right now.

finalDaemonChoice.summary: Keep the detached daemon as an internal private subsystem of the native CLI and preserve acquire/status/release plus TTL reuse semantics.
reasons: Keeping the daemon preserves the existing browser-info diagnostic model, including the direct /health and /browser/acquire path.
The detached lifecycle continues to isolate long-lived browser ownership from short-lived CLI invocations, which fits the one-JSON-envelope machine contract.
Replacing or folding the daemon now would expand the migration scope before parity, contract, and release automation are in place.
